name: colonies
title: Colony Composite — HPC Scaling Readiness
description:
Two-study investigation to certify the colony composite for HPC
deployment.

Study 1 — colonies-01-hpc-readiness (this study):
  Build phase: fix daughter-process hydration so structural _add
  instantiates daughter EcoliWCMs through the composite engine.
  Decide phase: N-sweep (N ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8}) on one machine to
  extract per-cell wall-time + RSS scaling and identify the
  bottleneck. Produces a recommended cells/process and
  cells/HPC-node budget.

Study 2 — colonies-02-hpc-deployment (planned):
  Cross-node validation of the projected sizing. Run the
  recommended cells-per-process count across many processes on
  one HPC node, then across multiple nodes; confirm per-cell wall
  stays within ±20% of the laptop projection and that biology is
  consistent between distributed configurations.
question:
How many whole-cell E. coli agents can we fit per HPC node, and at
what per-cell wall-time cost, so that a colonies-on-HPC workload is
realistic to plan against? More fundamentally: does the multi-cell
colony composite (each cell embedding the full 55-process WCM via
EcoliWCM) actually support clean parallel growth + division at
scale, or are there per-cell-cost or per-cell-RAM cliffs that show
up only at N > 1?
hypothesis:
After fixing daughter-process hydration, the colony composite scales
linearly with N (per-cell wall ≈ constant, per-cell RAM ≈ constant)
on a single machine for N up to at least 8, and the dominant cost
is the inner EcoliWCM (not pymunk or scheduler). HPC sizing is then
a function of (RAM_per_node / RAM_per_cell, cores_per_node /
cells_per_process_at_realtime). The single bottleneck visible at
laptop scale will be the Python GIL — process-bigraph composites
are single-threaded by design, so HPC scaling means scaling
processes, not cells per process.

studies.name: colonies-01-hpc-readiness
studies.title: HPC scaling readiness for the colony composite
studies.question:
Is the pure whole-cell colony composite ready to scale on HPC?
Specifically: can N parallel EcoliWCMs grow and divide cleanly for
≥2 generations inside one composite, and how does wall-time / RAM /
per-tick cost scale with N on a single machine — well enough that
we can confidently project a cells-per-HPC-node budget?

findings.statement:
Per-cell wall time is flat at 70–74 ms across N ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8} (slight
DECREASE with N as Python/import overhead amortizes). Composite scales
linearly on one machine.

expected.summary: per-cell wall stays within 2× of the N=1 reference; flat is the strongest pass condition.

findings.next_action: Use 73 ms/tick/cell as the projection input for colonies-02-hpc-deployment.

findings.statement:
The GIL is the dominant bottleneck at colony scale. Process-bigraph
composites are single-threaded by design — one process uses ~1 CPU core
regardless of how many cells it holds. Scaling means more processes, not
more cells/process.

evidence.observed: pymunk_step_ms ≈ 0.1 ms/tick (free); ecoli_ms grows linearly with N

findings.explanation:
All 55 inner WCM steps are walked sequentially in one Python thread.
pymunk is free even at N=8, so any super-linear cost would have to be in
the EcoliWCM update — but per-cell stays flat. The only ceiling visible
is total wall vs realtime per process, which crosses ~1.0 around N≈13.

findings.statement:
Steady-state per-cell RSS is ~450 MB, atop a ~1 GB Python baseline
(ParCa + WCM imports + cached numpy arrays).

expected.summary:
Linear in N up to N=8 within one process. Sets the per-node cell
ceiling on HPC: 6 cells/process × 64 processes = ~290 GB on a 256 GB
node; drop to 5-6 cells/process for headroom → ~384 cells/node.

findings.statement:
pymunk 2D physics is essentially free at the N values we tested
(≤ 0.2 ms/tick at N=8). All wall-time cost is the inner EcoliWCM.

Three independent bugs blocked daughter hydration through the engine
and had to be fixed before the Decide phase could run.
findings.explanation:
(1) viva-munk apply_updates_with_realize unpacked 2 values from
bigraph_schema.core.realize, which now returns 3 (escape_merges) —
every structural _add crashed.
(2) v2ecoli/colony.py wired only mass/volume/exchange outputs on
initial cells; _handle_division writes to `agents` with no wire,
so mother updates had nowhere to land.
(3) v2ecoli/bridge.py _handle_division hard-coded `interval=60.0` for
daughters; `interval` is not in config_schema, so daughters ticked
once per 60s instead of inheriting the mother's 1s cadence.

evidence.observed: After all three fixes, pure-WC N=2 force-divided to 4 hydrated daughters that all advance on the next tick.

findings.statement:
RSS grows continuously during a single long N=1 run at ~5 MB/sim-second
(1126 MB at tick 0 → 7016 MB by tick 1050, before division). Indicates
either accumulating state in the EcoliWCM internal composite or a leak;
visible only in long runs, not in the 60s N-sweep windows.

evidence.observed: rss_mb climbs monotonically across the pre-division window

findings.next_action:
Folded into multi-gen-perf-drift follow-up — quantify drift over
natural divisions and isolate the source (cache, history, fragmentation).
